sections.h2: A large city with very different neighborhoods
sections.html:
Chesapeake sits in Hampton Roads as an independent city, second only to one other Virginia city in land area. It spans about 351 square miles, roughly 338 of them land. Residents numbered 249,422 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 255,332, which also ranks it second in the state for population.

A lot of that land is protected farmland, forest and wetland, including part of the Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge, so one address might be on a dense street near Norfolk and another on a rural road near the North Carolina line. Buyers who know Great Bridge may know little about Deep Creek or Western Branch. The old communities of South Norfolk, Butts Road, Deep Creek, Pleasant Grove, Western Branch and Washington each have their own character, and the same repair problem can be read differently in each.

sections.h2: Housing age and what it means for repairs
sections.html:
The city came together in 1963 when South Norfolk and the rest of Norfolk County consolidated. For decades much of it was suburban or rural, a bedroom community for Norfolk and Virginia Beach, and growth in the 1990s added roads, schools and water demand. Houses built in different decades therefore carry different systems, lot sizes and repair histories.

Older South Norfolk and Deep Creek homes often have deferred maintenance. Newer subdivisions have their own questions, such as drainage and age of the roof. When we look at a house, the build year and the neighborhood tell us where to start.

sections.h2: Water, flood zones and the crawl space
sections.html:
Humid summers and mild winters bring roughly 48 inches of precipitation a year. The land sits only about 16 feet above sea level among tidal rivers, canals and swamp. That makes drainage the most common selling problem here: a damp crawl space, standing water after heavy rain, or a lot that floods. Buyers and appraisers scrutinize all of it, and it is a frequent reason a listed house sits.

  • Check the crawl space for standing water, rot in the floor framing and failed vapor barriers.
  • Look at gutters and grading, and note any sump or French drain that has been added.
  • Ask the city or your insurer about the flood zone before you set a price, because flood status affects what a financed buyer can insure.
  • Record the roof's age. Humid summers and storm winds wear shingles out faster.

Drinking water comes mostly from the Northwest River and is treated with reverse osmosis because the river can run salty. The region also draws from Lake Gaston through a 76 mile pipeline. None of that changes a sale, but it explains why you may hear buyers ask about water quality.

Interstate 64 forms part of the Hampton Roads Beltway through the city, I-464 links to downtown Norfolk and Portsmouth, and I-664 heads toward Newport News. U.S. 13, 17, 58 and 460 cross the city, and State Route 168 includes the Chesapeake Expressway toll road. The city maintains 90 bridges and overpasses, five of them drawbridges that open an estimated 30,000 times a year, so rush hour feels different from one address to the next. Hampton Roads Transit buses run here, and Norfolk International is the nearest commercial airport.

Two Navy sites lie inside the city, Northwest Annex and Naval Auxiliary Landing Field Fentress. Public schools and city government are the biggest employers, and owners transferring out, retiring or settling an estate often sell on a schedule set by a job or a posting.

sections.h2: Real estate tax bills and due dates
sections.html:
Bills come four times a year, and the assessed figure is 100 percent of fair market value.

InstallmentDue date
FirstSeptember 30
SecondDecember 31
ThirdMarch 31
FourthJune 5

Call the City Real Estate Assessor, 757-382-6235, about how your property was valued. Tax relief for disabled owners and seniors has a May 15 application deadline, and the city also runs separate programs for surviving spouses and disabled owners who served. Council resets the rate yearly, so the Local Tax Rates page beats an old bill.

sections.h2: Taxes and transfer costs at closing
sections.html:
Under state law a tax bill nobody paid turns into a lien that jumps the line ahead of other claims, and it sits on the property until the locality has its money. Whoever covers which days of the tax year is spelled out in your purchase contract.

Expect to pay a grantor tax too, at 50 cents on every $500 of the price, unless buyer and seller agree to split it differently. The deed's first page must show the price, and the clerk of court takes the tax when the deed is recorded. Settle these early:

  • Ask the Treasurer what an unpaid installment would cost to clear.
  • Agree on paper who bears the grantor tax and recording fees.
  • Ask the title company to look for liens, judgments and overdue utility bills.
  • For an estate property, find out who is entitled to sign the deed.

Most Chesapeake sellers who contact us are dealing with the house itself rather than the market. Water damage from low ground, deferred repairs and tenant-occupied properties come up again and again.

  • An inherited house that nobody lives in, with taxes and insurance still due.
  • Rot, mold or moisture that would block standard financing.
  • A military or civilian transfer on a short timeline.
  • A rental with a tenant or a lapsed lease.

Because the house is bought in whatever shape it is in, nobody asks you to repair, stage or show it. Depending on the property, we buy it ourselves or bring a vetted cash buyer, and we say which when the offer arrives. Listing remains an option to compare.

sections.h2: What to expect from the process
sections.html:
Start by describing the house and anything wrong with it. Our written offer follows. After you accept, a local title company opens a file, hunts for liens, and drafts the deed and settlement statement. You mostly choose the closing day, since no underwriter sets a deadline. When title is clean, a few weeks is realistic; liens or estate paperwork stretch that.

Owners who live elsewhere, including military families who have moved, can finish the sale remotely with signed documents. Two phone calls help before signing: the Treasurer for balances, and the assessor if the valuation looks wrong.

Keep the paperwork handy as well. Your latest tax bill, the deed, any insurance claims for water damage and a list of repairs you already made all help us price the house fairly and help the title company move faster. If a tenant lives there, tell us the lease terms at the start so nothing surprises anyone at closing.

faqs.q: How fast can I sell my house in Chesapeake for cash?
faqs.a: Mostly on title and the date you pick. Without a lender, the wait is the title company clearing the file, often a few weeks. Liens or estate paperwork can push it out.

faqs.q: When are Chesapeake real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: Four installments fall on September 30, December 31, March 31 and June 5. Anything still owed at closing is paid from your proceeds, so get the figure from the Treasurer's office first.

faqs.q: Does Virginia charge a tax when I sell a house?
faqs.a: Yes. The seller usually pays a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 of the price, though the contract can change that. Your settlement statement lists the amount.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Chesapeake house that is in a flood zone or has water damage?
faqs.a: Yes. Moisture trouble or a poor crawl space does not rule out a cash buyer, though the offer will account for repairs. Flood status mostly hurts a financed buyer who needs insurance.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my assessment in Chesapeake?
faqs.a: The City Real Estate Assessor, at 757-382-6235, can walk you through the valuation, which is set at 100 percent of fair market value.
